# Part 2 — Citation graph: structural descriptions

```{r}
#| label: install
#| eval: false
install.packages(c("igraph", "tidyverse", "ggraph", "tidygraph", "jsonlite"))
```

```{r}
#| label: libraries
library(igraph)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggraph)
library(tidygraph)
library(jsonlite)
library(here)
```

```{r}
#| label: load-graph
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
edges <- read_csv(here("data", "citation_edgelist.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
g <- graph_from_data_frame(edges, directed = TRUE)

bib <- fromJSON(here("data", "bibliography.json"), simplifyDataFrame = FALSE)

# Active entries only (tombstoned entries are excluded from the export,
# but guard here in case of an older bibliography file). Note: entries
# tombstoned via `delete` (not `merge`) that appear as a citer elsewhere
# are retained in the edge list so their outbound edges aren't lost — see
# exporter.py and docs/methods/corrections-system.md. Ghost nodes have no
# reliable bibliographic metadata; they are kept in the graph (their edges
# are real) but excluded from any display table or join that assumes real
# title/author/topic data.
bib <- bib[!sapply(bib, function(e) isTRUE(e[["_deleted"]]))]

node_attrs <- tibble(
  name            = names(bib),
  title           = map_chr(bib, ~ .x$title %||% ""),
  year            = map_chr(bib, ~ .x$date %||% .x$year %||% ""),
  generation      = map_chr(bib, ~ .x$generation %||% ""),
  entry_type      = map_chr(bib, ~ .x$entry_type %||% ""),
  resolution      = map_chr(bib, ~ .x[["_resolution_method"]] %||% "grobid"),
  completeness    = map_chr(bib, ~ .x$completeness$label %||% ""),
  # author is a list of {family, given} objects per entry (or NULL/empty
  # for entries GROBID/the LLM couldn't resolve an author for); flattened
  # here to a single "Family, Family" display string, since this is only
  # used for display (tooltips, tables) and never joined or filtered on.
  author          = map_chr(bib, function(e) {
    au <- e$author
    if (is.null(au) || length(au) == 0) return("")
    paste(map_chr(au, ~ .x$family %||% ""), collapse = ", ")
  }),
)

# Ghost = a node present in the edge list (it cites or is cited by
# something) but absent from the active bibliography — i.e. no real
# metadata to join. Derived from edge-list membership rather than a
# GraphML attribute, since we're not loading GraphML at all (libxml2
# isn't installable here without sudo — see gn_analysis/README.md for
# the same constraint on the GN side).
is_ghost <- tibble(
  name     = V(g)$name,
  is_ghost = if_else(V(g)$name %in% node_attrs$name, "false", "true")
)

gn_ghost_count <- sum(is_ghost$is_ghost == "true")
```

```{r}
#| label: components
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
wcc <- components(g, mode = "weak")
scc <- components(g, mode = "strong")

gn_wcc_pct <- round(100 * max(wcc$csize) / vcount(g), 1)

V(g)$component_weak   <- wcc$membership
V(g)$component_strong <- scc$membership
```

## Graph summary

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Nodes | `r format(vcount(g), big.mark = ",")` |
| Edges | `r format(ecount(g), big.mark = ",")` |
| Directed | Yes |
| Density[^density] | `r format(edge_density(g), scientific = FALSE)` |
| Weakly connected components[^wcc] | `r format(wcc$no, big.mark = ",")` |
| Largest weak component | `r format(max(wcc$csize), big.mark = ",")` nodes (`r gn_wcc_pct`% of graph) |
| Strongly connected components[^scc] | `r format(scc$no, big.mark = ",")` |
| Largest strong component | `r format(max(scc$csize), big.mark = ",")` nodes |

[^density]: The proportion of possible edges that actually exist: edges
  present divided by every pair of nodes that *could* be connected. Low
  density is normal and expected for a citation network — most works
  don't cite most other works.

[^wcc]: A weakly connected component treats every edge as undirected: two
  nodes are in the same component if a path connects them in either
  citation direction. This is the more forgiving of the two measures
  here.

[^scc]: A strongly connected component requires an actual directed path
  in *both* directions between two nodes. Rare in citation networks,
  since citations are historically directed — a 2010 paper cannot cite
  a 2020 paper — so most strongly connected components are single
  isolated nodes.

## Degree and centrality

In-degree (times cited within the corpus) and out-degree (number of works
cited) capture different roles. High in-degree identifies widely-cited works
— the intellectual anchors of the field. High out-degree identifies works
that are heavily engaged with the literature, drawing on many sources.

Betweenness centrality identifies works that sit on many shortest paths
between other works — brokers between sub-literatures. Betweenness is
expensive to compute on large graphs; both normalized and raw values are
reported. Normalized divides by the theoretical maximum for a graph this
size (roughly (n-1)(n-2) for a directed graph), so on a graph with over
12,000 nodes even a genuinely high-betweenness work normalizes to a very
small fraction — small in absolute terms, not because the work is
unimportant. Raw values, not rescaled, are more intuitively legible for
comparing works directly against each other.

PageRank assigns authority based on incoming links weighted by the
authority of the linking node — conceptually similar to being cited by
works that are themselves widely cited. Hub and authority scores (HITS)
are complementary: hubs point to many authorities; authorities are pointed
to by many hubs.

Peripheral works — low degree, low centrality by every measure below — are
not treated as noise in this project. A work cited only once may be exactly
the interesting case (a niche, contested, or newly emerging reference) for
a study of citational politics. No node is excluded from any measure in
this section on the basis of low degree.

```{r}
#| label: degree
V(g)$degree_in  <- degree(g, mode = "in")
V(g)$degree_out <- degree(g, mode = "out")
V(g)$degree_all <- degree(g, mode = "all")
```

```{r}
#| label: centrality
V(g)$betweenness      <- betweenness(g, directed = TRUE, normalized = TRUE)
V(g)$betweenness_raw  <- betweenness(g, directed = TRUE, normalized = FALSE)
V(g)$closeness_in <- closeness(g, mode = "in", normalized = TRUE)
V(g)$pagerank     <- page_rank(g, directed = TRUE)$vector
V(g)$hub          <- hub_score(g)$vector
V(g)$authority    <- authority_score(g)$vector

centrality_df <- tibble(
  name            = V(g)$name,
  betweenness     = V(g)$betweenness,
  betweenness_raw = V(g)$betweenness_raw,
  closeness   = V(g)$closeness_in,
  pagerank    = V(g)$pagerank,
  hub         = V(g)$hub,
  authority   = V(g)$authority,
  in_degree   = V(g)$degree_in,
  out_degree  = V(g)$degree_out,
  degree      = V(g)$degree_all,
) |> left_join(node_attrs, by = "name") |> left_join(is_ghost, by = "name")
```

### Most cited (by in-degree)

```{r}
centrality_df |>
  filter(is_ghost == "false") |>
  arrange(desc(in_degree)) |>
  head(20) |>
  select(name, title, year, generation, in_degree) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

### Most citing (by out-degree)

```{r}
centrality_df |>
  filter(is_ghost == "false") |>
  arrange(desc(out_degree)) |>
  head(20) |>
  select(name, title, year, generation, out_degree) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

### Degree distribution

A power-law or scale-free degree distribution is characteristic of citation
networks: most works are cited rarely, a small number are cited frequently,
visible as a roughly straight-line decline on a log-log plot. The plot below
tests whether this corpus follows that pattern.

```{r}
#| label: degree-dist
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(centrality_df, aes(x = in_degree)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = log10(in_degree)), bins = 20, fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = function(x) round(10^x),
    name = "In-degree (times cited)"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "In-degree distribution (log-log)",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The bulk of the distribution (in-degree 1 through roughly 8) follows a
fairly straight decline on this log-log scale, consistent with the
expected power-law pattern: most works are cited once or twice, a much
smaller number several times. The tail is real, not an artifact of a
truncated plot axis: the maximum in-degree in this corpus is
`r max(centrality_df$in_degree, na.rm = TRUE)`. A handful of works drive
that high-citation tail, listed below rather than relied on to show
clearly as bars on the histogram above, since bars this sparse are easy
to miss regardless of binning.

### Most-cited works (the high end of the tail)

The most-cited works in this corpus, driving the sparse, high-in-degree
tail visible in the plot above:

```{r}
#| label: degree-dist-tail
centrality_df |>
  filter(in_degree > 30) |>
  select(name, title, year, in_degree) |>
  arrange(desc(in_degree)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

### Top by betweenness centrality

Works with high betweenness mediate between otherwise disconnected parts
of the citation network — likely works that bridge sub-fields or periods.
"Bridges" below lists the top 3 Girvan-Newman clusters (by count) found
among each work's direct citations and citers, with the number of
neighbors in each — a broker connecting mostly to one cluster and only
incidentally to others will show that concentration, rather than an
undifferentiated list of every cluster it happens to touch (see
"Girvan-Newman communities" and "Cluster labeling" further down for how
those labels are produced; a self-contained lookup here, independent of
that later section, so this table isn't affected by whether cluster
labelling has been run).

```{r}
#| label: betweenness-bridges
# Self-contained: finds the same fragmentation-onset partition file the
# "Girvan-Newman communities" section uses later, and reads
# cluster_labelling/results/cluster_labels.csv directly here rather than
# depending on gn_cluster_labels (defined further down) — this chunk does
# not move or duplicate that later code, it just reads the same
# already-on-disk files independently, since both exist regardless of
# where in this document they're referenced.
bw_multi_cut_dir <- here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "multi_cut")
bw_cut_files <- if (dir.exists(bw_multi_cut_dir)) {
  list.files(bw_multi_cut_dir, pattern = "^communities_round_[0-9]+\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
} else character(0)

bw_bridges <- tibble(name = character(), bridges = character())

if (length(bw_cut_files) > 0) {
  bw_rounds <- as.integer(gsub(".*communities_round_([0-9]+)\\.csv$", "\\1", bw_cut_files))
  bw_partition <- read_csv(bw_cut_files[which.min(bw_rounds)], show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    rename(community_gn = community_id)

  bw_labels_path <- here("analysis", "cluster_labelling", "results", "cluster_labels.csv")
  bw_labels <- if (file.exists(bw_labels_path)) {
    read_csv(bw_labels_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
      mutate(community_id = as.character(community_id)) |>
      select(community_id, label)
  } else {
    tibble(community_id = character(), label = character())
  }

  bw_node_labels <- bw_partition |>
    mutate(community_gn = as.character(community_gn)) |>
    left_join(bw_labels, by = c("community_gn" = "community_id")) |>
    mutate(label = coalesce(label, paste0("Community ", community_gn)))

  # For each top-betweenness node: pull its direct in- and out-neighbors
  # from the raw graph, look up each neighbor's cluster label, and list
  # the distinct labels found — this is "what it's bridging," not just
  # "where it itself sits" (its own community_gn would answer a
  # different question).
  bw_top_names <- centrality_df |>
    filter(is_ghost == "false") |>
    arrange(desc(betweenness)) |>
    head(20) |>
    pull(name)

  bw_bridges <- map_dfr(bw_top_names, function(nm) {
    neighbor_ids <- unique(c(
      names(igraph::neighbors(g, nm, mode = "in")),
      names(igraph::neighbors(g, nm, mode = "out"))
    ))
    # Ranked by how many of this node's neighbors actually sit in each
    # cluster, not alphabetically: a broker connecting to 8 neighbors in
    # one cluster and 1 each in several others is mostly bridging INTO
    # that first cluster, and an alphabetical list treats all of them as
    # equally relevant, which they aren't. Capped at the top 3 to keep
    # the column readable — a highly-connected broker can otherwise touch
    # a dozen or more distinct clusters, most of them via a single
    # incidental neighbor.
    neighbor_label_counts <- bw_node_labels |>
      filter(node_id %in% neighbor_ids) |>
      count(label, sort = TRUE)
    top_labels <- neighbor_label_counts |>
      slice_head(n = 3) |>
      mutate(display = paste0(label, " (", n, ")"))
    n_more <- nrow(neighbor_label_counts) - nrow(top_labels)
    bridges_text <- if (nrow(top_labels) == 0) {
      ""
    } else {
      paste0(
        paste(top_labels$display, collapse = "; "),
        if (n_more > 0) paste0("; +", n_more, " more") else ""
      )
    }
    tibble(name = nm, bridges = bridges_text)
  })
}

centrality_df |>
  filter(is_ghost == "false") |>
  arrange(desc(betweenness)) |>
  head(20) |>
  select(name, title, year, betweenness, betweenness_raw) |>
  left_join(bw_bridges, by = "name") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

### Betweenness and publication year

A negative relationship between publication year and betweenness is
expected as a baseline structural effect, independent of any specific
work's importance: an older work has had more time to accumulate
citations from both earlier and later literature, giving it more
opportunities to sit on shortest paths between clusters that didn't yet
exist when it was published. The interesting question is not whether
that baseline trend exists, but what departs from it: works that are old
without being especially well-connected, and, more notably, works that
are young but already bridging despite limited time to accumulate
citations — those are candidates for genuinely novel synthesis, not just
structurally advantaged age.

```{r}
#| label: betweenness-year
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
bw_year_df <- centrality_df |>
  filter(is_ghost == "false") |>
  # year is free-text, sourced from bibliography metadata (dates, ranges,
  # and circa notation all appear there) — this pulls the first 4-digit
  # run found, a pragmatic extraction, not a full date parser. Works with
  # no recognizable 4-digit year are dropped below rather than guessed at.
  mutate(year_numeric = suppressWarnings(as.integer(str_extract(year, "\\d{4}"))))

bw_n_total <- nrow(bw_year_df)
bw_n_no_year <- sum(is.na(bw_year_df$year_numeric))
bw_n_zero_bw <- sum(!is.na(bw_year_df$year_numeric) & bw_year_df$betweenness_raw == 0)

# Zero betweenness is the normal, expected state for most works in a
# sparse citation graph (only a work that actually sits on a shortest
# path between some other pair has nonzero betweenness at all) — it is
# not a data problem, and excluding it here is not hiding anything.
# Plotting all ~12,600 works, most sitting at zero, was tried and found
# to make the plot unreadable: the zero-betweenness mass visually
# dominates the chart and compresses the actual signal, the nonzero
# points, into an illegible corner. This plot keeps only the nonzero
# subset, where there's an actual distribution to look at.
bw_year_df <- bw_year_df |>
  filter(!is.na(year_numeric), betweenness_raw > 0)

ggplot(bw_year_df, aes(x = year_numeric, y = betweenness_raw)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", colour = "firebrick", se = TRUE) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Betweenness (raw) by publication year, nonzero works only",
    subtitle = paste0(
      nrow(bw_year_df), " of ", format(bw_n_total, big.mark = ","),
      " works are shown here: works with zero betweenness (",
      format(bw_n_zero_bw, big.mark = ","), " of them, the normal state ",
      "for most works in a sparse citation graph, not excluded data) and ",
      "works with no parseable year (", bw_n_no_year, ") are left out."
    ),
    x = "Publication year", y = "Betweenness (raw, log scale)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The trend line[^loess] is fit to this nonzero subset, where the
actual bridging signal is. On this corpus, betweenness is concentrated
almost entirely in works from roughly 2000 onward: the x-axis above is
effectively empty before that point, since essentially no pre-2000 work
in this corpus has nonzero betweenness at all. This isn't simply "older
works have lower betweenness" as a gradient; it's closer to a hard
boundary, worth seeing directly rather than taking on faith: the plot
below shows every work, including the zero-betweenness majority, so the
boundary itself is visible rather than described secondhand.

```{r}
#| label: betweenness-year-full
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
# betweenness_raw + 1 is plotted, not betweenness_raw, since a true log
# scale can't display a zero: every zero maps to 1 (log10(1) = 0, a
# real, visible position at the bottom of the axis), and every nonzero
# value keeps its actual relative position, shifted by a negligible one
# unit. geom_jitter (x-only, height = 0) rather than geom_point, since
# thousands of exact-zero points would otherwise stack into one solid,
# uninformative line; the horizontal jitter lets their real density per
# year remain visible.
ggplot(centrality_df |>
         filter(is_ghost == "false") |>
         mutate(year_numeric = suppressWarnings(as.integer(str_extract(year, "\\d{4}")))) |>
         filter(!is.na(year_numeric)),
       aes(x = year_numeric, y = betweenness_raw + 1)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.3, height = 0, alpha = 0.15, colour = "steelblue") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Betweenness (raw + 1) by publication year, every work",
    subtitle = "The boundary itself: a dense mass of zero-betweenness works across every year, and a nonzero cloud confined almost entirely to the right edge, from roughly 2000 onward.",
    x = "Publication year", y = "Betweenness (raw + 1, log scale)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Whether the boundary reflects something about the corpus itself (older
material may be primary sources, sagas, or editions with different
citation patterns than modern academic synthesis) or a genuine
historiographical shift (post-2000 archaeology being where cross-cutting
synthesis actually happens) can't be settled from either plot alone.

[^loess]: A LOESS fit, not a strict linear one, to allow for a
  non-constant relationship across the full year range rather than
  forcing a single slope.

## Connected components

A dominant giant weak component indicates a well-connected literature;
summary figures are in the Graph summary table above. On this corpus,
that dominance is complete: every node belongs to a single weakly
connected component of `r format(vcount(g), big.mark = ",")` nodes, with
no isolated fragments.

## K-core decomposition

The k-core of a graph is the maximal subgraph in which every node has at
least k connections to other nodes within that subgraph. It is computed by
iteratively removing nodes with degree below k until no further removal
is possible. A node's **coreness** is the highest k for which it still
belongs to the k-core: a coreness of 1 means the node only survives the
weakest possible core (removed as soon as k reaches 2), while a high
coreness means the node stays embedded even as the graph is stripped down
to only its most densely-interconnected parts.

K-core decomposition is reported here purely as a **descriptive**
measure, showing which works sit in dense mutual-citation relationships
versus which sit at the periphery, following @alvarezhamelin2005. Every
work, regardless of its coreness, is still included in full in every
other analysis in this document: coreness only describes a work's
position, it doesn't filter anything out.

Coreness and in-degree measure genuinely different things, worth
comparing directly: in-degree simply counts how many times a work is
cited, with no regard for whether those citing works are themselves
well-connected. Coreness asks a structurally deeper question, whether a
work sits inside a neighborhood that is *itself* densely interconnected,
not just cited often in isolation. A work could have high in-degree
while sitting at low coreness, if most of its citations come from
otherwise peripheral, poorly-connected works; conversely, a work with
only moderate in-degree can have high coreness if it's embedded in a
tightly interlinked core. The tables below show whether these two
measures broadly agree on this corpus, or diverge in informative ways.

```{r}
#| label: kcore
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
g_undirected <- as_undirected(g, mode = "collapse")
V(g)$coreness <- coreness(g_undirected)

centrality_df <- centrality_df |>
  left_join(tibble(name = V(g)$name, coreness = V(g)$coreness), by = "name")
```

```{r}
#| label: kcore-table
#| echo: false
centrality_df |>
  group_by(coreness) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_in_degree = mean(in_degree)) |>
  arrange(desc(coreness)) |>
  head(15) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: kcore-top
centrality_df |>
  filter(is_ghost == "false") |>
  arrange(desc(coreness), desc(in_degree)) |>
  head(20) |>
  select(name, title, year, coreness, in_degree) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The top of the coreness = 9 core is, essentially, the same five works
identified earlier as the tail of the in-degree distribution and the
highest-betweenness bridges: `price2002`, `skre2007`, `svanberg2003`,
`sindbaek2007`, `brink2008`. Three independent structural measures,
in-degree, betweenness, and k-core, converge on the same small set of
works, which is a stronger, cross-validated signal than any one measure
alone: these works aren't merely well-cited or merely well-positioned by
one particular definition of centrality, they're structurally central by
several different, genuinely distinct criteria at once.

## Community detection

Community detection here produces several independent descriptions of how
the graph divides, not a single answer to be triangulated. Louvain
[@blondel2008] and Leiden [@traag2019] ask "which groups of nodes are more
densely interconnected than a random graph with the same degree sequence
would predict," a notion formalized as modularity [@newman2006].
Girvan-Newman [@girvan2002] asks "which edges, if removed, disconnect
otherwise-separate parts of the network." These are genuinely different
questions; neither validates the other. K-means, below, adds a third,
differently-grounded description again: not by graph structure at all,
but by each work's centrality profile, grouping works that occupy
similar structural positions, for example highly-cited authorities vs.
high-betweenness brokers vs. peripheral works.

### Louvain

```{r}
#| label: louvain
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
louvain <- cluster_louvain(g_undirected)
V(g)$community_louvain <- membership(louvain)
gn_louvain_n <- length(louvain)
gn_louvain_modularity <- round(modularity(louvain), 4)
```

Louvain finds `r format(gn_louvain_n, big.mark = ",")` communities, at
a modularity of `r gn_louvain_modularity`. The 20 largest:

```{r}
#| label: louvain-table
#| echo: false
tibble(community = seq_along(sizes(louvain)), size = sizes(louvain)) |>
  arrange(desc(size)) |>
  head(20) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: louvain-viz
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 12
#| cache: true
tg <- as_tbl_graph(g) |>
  activate(nodes) |>
  mutate(community = as.factor(V(g)$community_louvain))

ggraph(tg, layout = "drl") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.05, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = community), size = 0.3, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(guide = "none") +
  theme_graph() +
  labs(title = "Citation graph — Louvain communities")

ggsave("bibvik_louvain.png", width = 16, height = 16, dpi = 300)
ggsave("bibvik_louvain.pdf", width = 16, height = 16, device = cairo_pdf)
```

### Leiden

```{r}
#| label: leiden
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
leiden <- cluster_leiden(g_undirected, objective_function = "modularity")
leiden_membership <- as.integer(membership(leiden))
V(g)$community_leiden <- leiden_membership
gn_leiden_n <- length(leiden)
gn_leiden_modularity <- round(modularity(g_undirected, leiden_membership), 4)
```

Leiden finds `r format(gn_leiden_n, big.mark = ",")` communities, at a
modularity of `r gn_leiden_modularity`. The 20 largest:

```{r}
#| label: leiden-table
#| echo: false
tibble(community = seq_along(sizes(leiden)), size = sizes(leiden)) |>
  arrange(desc(size)) |>
  head(20) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: leiden-viz
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 12
#| cache: true
tg <- as_tbl_graph(g) |>
  activate(nodes) |>
  mutate(community = as.factor(V(g)$community_leiden))

ggraph(tg, layout = "drl") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.05, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = community), size = 0.3, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(guide = "none") +
  theme_graph() +
  labs(title = "Citation graph — Leiden communities")

ggsave("bibvik_leiden.png", width = 16, height = 16, dpi = 300)
ggsave("bibvik_leiden.pdf", width = 16, height = 16, device = cairo_pdf)
```

```{r}
#| label: export-structural
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
node_table <- centrality_df |>
  left_join(
    tibble(
      name              = V(g)$name,
      coreness          = V(g)$coreness,
      component_weak    = V(g)$component_weak,
      component_strong  = V(g)$component_strong,
      community_louvain = V(g)$community_louvain,
      community_leiden  = V(g)$community_leiden,
      cluster_kmeans    = V(g)$cluster_kmeans,
    ),
    by = "name"
  )

# Girvan-Newman communities are computed standalone (see gn_analysis/)
# and joined in here only if available. communities.csv (written by
# run_gn_analysis.R) holds the best-modularity cut, which on this
# corpus is 97.5% singletons and not usable — see the write-up below.
# The partition actually joined here is the earliest fragmentation-onset
# cut from gn_analysis/results/multi_cut/, produced by
# generate_multi_cut_communities.R. That directory holds one file per
# detected onset round; the earliest (smallest round number) is the one
# established below as usable, so it's selected by sorting rather than
# a hardcoded round number, in case a future re-run shifts which rounds
# qualify.
gn_multi_cut_dir <- here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "multi_cut")
gn_cut_files <- if (dir.exists(gn_multi_cut_dir)) {
  list.files(gn_multi_cut_dir, pattern = "^communities_round_[0-9]+\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
} else {
  character(0)
}

# Full onset-round summary table, for soft-coding every round/count/
# percentage figure quoted in the prose below via inline `r` expressions
# rather than hand-typed numbers that go stale on re-render.
gn_summary_path <- file.path(gn_multi_cut_dir, "multi_cut_summary.csv")
gn_summary <- if (file.exists(gn_summary_path)) {
  read_csv(gn_summary_path) |>
    mutate(pct_singleton = n_singletons / n_communities) |>
    arrange(round)
} else {
  tibble(round = integer(), n_communities = integer(),
         n_singletons = integer(), largest_community = integer(),
         pct_singleton = double())
}
gn_earliest <- if (nrow(gn_summary) > 0) gn_summary |> slice(1) else NULL
gn_latest   <- if (nrow(gn_summary) > 0) gn_summary |> slice(n()) else NULL

if (length(gn_cut_files) > 0) {
  gn_rounds <- as.integer(gsub(".*communities_round_([0-9]+)\\.csv$", "\\1", gn_cut_files))
  gn_result_path <- gn_cut_files[which.min(gn_rounds)]
  gn_communities <- read_csv(gn_result_path) |>
    rename(community_gn = community_id)
  node_table <- node_table |> left_join(gn_communities, by = c("name" = "node_id"))
  cat("Joined Girvan-Newman communities from", gn_result_path,
      "(fragmentation-onset round", min(gn_rounds), ") \n")
} else {
  cat("No Girvan-Newman multi-cut results found at", gn_multi_cut_dir,
      "— run gn_analysis/generate_multi_cut_communities.R first. Skipping join.\n")
}

write_csv(node_table, "bibvik_node_table.csv")
cat("Written bibvik_node_table.csv\n")
cat("Rows:", nrow(node_table), "\n")

# Plain boolean, computed once here rather than repeated as a quoted
# expression in each downstream chunk's eval: guard — avoids YAML
# quoting issues with !expr and string literals.
gn_has_communities <- "community_gn" %in% colnames(node_table) && any(!is.na(node_table$community_gn))
```

### Girvan-Newman

This section covers a further way of dividing the graph into
communities by its structure, alongside Louvain and Leiden above, and
the specific problem that comes with it: unlike those two methods,
Girvan-Newman does not return a single answer, and one has to be
chosen from what it does produce.

Louvain and Leiden each partition the graph once, at one resolution,
and return a single result. Girvan-Newman [@girvan2002] instead removes
edges one at a time: at each step, it identifies the edge with the
highest betweenness centrality (the edge carrying the largest number of
shortest paths between all pairs of nodes in the graph), removes it,
and recomputes betweenness for the remaining edges before repeating.
Because a shortest path between two densely connected regions of a
graph usually has to cross whichever single edge joins them, that edge
tends to have disproportionately high betweenness and is removed
early, while edges internal to a well-connected region, which have
many alternative paths around them, are removed only much later. The
result is a record of the entire removal sequence, from the original,
fully connected graph down to every paper standing alone: a
dendrogram. The tree below is that record. Height represents the order
in which components split apart, not the raw round number, since the
actual rounds are spaced too unevenly to remain legible on a linear
axis; left-right position carries no information and is arranged only
to avoid crossing branches.

```{r}
#| label: gn-dendrogram-generate
#| eval: !expr gn_has_communities
#| results: hide
gn_dendrogram_dir <- here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "dendrogram")
gn_dendrogram_png <- file.path(gn_dendrogram_dir, "gn_dendrogram.png")

# Regenerated whenever missing or older than the removal log it's
# built from, so a fresh GN run is reflected without a manual step,
# but re-rendering right after an unrelated edit doesn't re-run this
# multi-minute build for no reason.
gn_removal_log <- here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "removal_log.csv")
gn_dendrogram_stale <- !file.exists(gn_dendrogram_png) ||
  file.info(gn_dendrogram_png)$mtime < file.info(gn_removal_log)$mtime

if (gn_dendrogram_stale) {
  dir.create(gn_dendrogram_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  status <- system2(
    "Rscript",
    args = c(
      here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "build_dendrogram.R"),
      here("data", "citation_edgelist.csv"),
      gn_removal_log,
      gn_dendrogram_dir,
      "300", "0", "0",
      here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "modularity_trace.csv")
    )
  )
  if (status != 0) {
    warning("build_dendrogram.R exited with status ", status,
            "; dendrogram figure may be missing or stale.")
  }
}
```

```{r}
#| label: gn-dendrogram-embed
#| eval: !expr file.exists(here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "dendrogram", "gn_dendrogram.png"))
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics(here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "dendrogram", "gn_dendrogram.png"))
```

Girvan-Newman, in its original form, does not select a stopping point
from this sequence [@fortunato2010]; the removal process continues
until no edges remain. A refinement published two years after the
original algorithm [@newman2004] selects the
round with the highest modularity score as the working partition, and
this is the conventional choice, but it fails on this corpus: modularity
continues to rise as the graph fragments, reaching its maximum only once
97.5% of nodes are singleton communities, which is not a usable
partition. This is a documented limitation of modularity on sparse
networks, where it can lack a clear maximum and instead admit many
different high-scoring partitions [@good2010]. The criterion used
instead counts connected components directly: the point where that
count starts climbing steadily, one round after another, marks where
the graph is actually breaking into pieces, independent of whether
modularity happens to be rising or falling at the same time. The
earliest such round, `r format(gn_earliest$round, big.mark = ",")`, is
used for every community grouping in the rest of this document.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Full trace

```{r}
#| label: gn-modularity-trace
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| eval: !expr file.exists(here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "modularity_trace.csv"))
gn_trace <- read_csv(
  here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "modularity_trace.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# One row per Girvan-Newman round, written directly by
# gn_analysis/run_gn_analysis.R (round, edges_removed, n_components,
# modularity) — the full trace, not the onset summary in the other
# tab (whatever number of rows that turns out to have). Two series on
# one plot, different scales (modularity is
# roughly 0-1, component count runs into the thousands as the graph
# fragments), so component count is rescaled onto modularity's range
# for display and given its own right-hand axis with the real numbers.
gn_component_scale <- max(gn_trace$n_components) / max(gn_trace$modularity, na.rm = TRUE)

gn_trace_plot <- ggplot(gn_trace, aes(x = round)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = modularity, colour = "Modularity")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = n_components / gn_component_scale, colour = "Connected components"))

# Onset rounds come from gn_summary (multi_cut_summary.csv), a
# different, independently-loaded source from gn_trace
# (modularity_trace.csv) — both are checked for rows before use, since
# either file can be present without the other.
if (nrow(gn_summary) > 0) {
  gn_trace_plot <- gn_trace_plot +
    geom_vline(xintercept = gn_summary$round, linetype = "dashed",
               colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.4)
}

gn_trace_plot +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Modularity",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . * gn_component_scale, name = "Connected components",
                         labels = function(x) format(x, big.mark = ","))
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Modularity" = "firebrick", "Connected components" = "steelblue"),
                       name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = "Modularity and fragmentation across the full Girvan-Newman run",
    subtitle = "Dashed lines mark the fragmentation-onset rounds in the other tab",
    x = "Round"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Every round of the run, not just the fragmentation-onset points: this
is where the modularity failure described above is visible directly,
rising for most of the run while the component count climbs into the
thousands. The dashed lines show where those onset points actually
fall relative to that trend, letting the two be read together rather
than as separate, disconnected figures.

## Fragmentation onsets

```{r gn-onset-table}
#| echo: false

gn_summary |>
  transmute(
    Round = format(round, big.mark = ","),
    Communities = format(n_communities, big.mark = ","),
```

The specific rounds the connected-components criterion identifies as
sustained fragmentation onsets, the discrete points the working
partition below is chosen from.

:::

```{r}
#| label: gn-setup
#| eval: !expr gn_has_communities
# Shared setup for both the interactive and static views below: which
# communities to highlight, their colours, and the annotated graph
# object. Computed once, here, so the interactive section (shown first
# for reading order) and the static plot (further down) draw from the
# same partition and colour scheme rather than risking drift between
# two separate copies of this logic.
#
# Community count colored individually via a continuous viridis scale
# is not legible: adjacent community IDs land on near-identical shades,
# so the plot reads as a handful of broad color bands rather than
# distinct groups (confirmed visually on a render of the previous
# corpus, at a similar community count). Highlighting only the
# largest communities in distinct colors, with everything else grey,
# shows the actual pattern in this partition instead: a handful of
# large communities against a long tail of small ones.
gn_top_n <- 20
top_gn_communities <- node_table |>
  filter(!is.na(community_gn)) |>
  count(community_gn, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = gn_top_n) |>
  pull(community_gn)

# Community fill uses a discrete HCL wheel, one hue per top community plus
# grey for everything else — legible up to ~20 communities. F1/F2 is
# shown as a separate visual channel (point border) rather than folded
# into this same color scale, since F1/F2 cuts across community
# membership rather than nesting inside it — conflating the two into
# one legend would misrepresent that relationship.
gn_community_colours <- c(
  "other" = "grey85",
  setNames(
    grDevices::hcl(h = seq(15, 375, length.out = gn_top_n + 1)[-(gn_top_n + 1)],
                    c = 100, l = 65),
    top_gn_communities
  )
)

# cluster_labelling/ (see analysis/cluster_labelling/README.md) is a
# separate, manually-run pipeline — not part of this render chain — so
# its output may or may not exist at render time. Read it if present,
# fall back to bare "Community N" if not, so this document never
# depends on that pipeline having been run. Only clusters that pipeline
# was pointed at (currently the top 25 by size) and that passed its
# stability check will have a real label; every other community still
# falls back to "Community N".
gn_cluster_labels_path <- here("analysis", "cluster_labelling", "results", "cluster_labels.csv")
gn_cluster_labels <- if (file.exists(gn_cluster_labels_path)) {
  read_csv(gn_cluster_labels_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    mutate(community_id = as.character(community_id)) |>
    select(community_id, cluster_label = label)
} else {
  tibble(community_id = character(), cluster_label = character())
}

tg <- as_tbl_graph(g) |>
  activate(nodes) |>
  left_join(node_table |> select(name, community_gn, generation), by = "name") |>
  mutate(
    community_gn_highlight = if_else(community_gn %in% top_gn_communities,
                                      as.character(community_gn), "other")
  ) |>
  left_join(gn_cluster_labels, by = c("community_gn_highlight" = "community_id")) |>
  mutate(
    community_gn_highlight = fct_relevel(community_gn_highlight, "other"),
    community_label = case_when(
      community_gn_highlight == "other" ~ "Other",
      !is.na(cluster_label) ~ cluster_label,
      TRUE ~ paste("Community", community_gn_highlight)
    ),
    community_label = fct_reorder(community_label, community_gn_highlight == "other"),
    is_f1 = !is.na(generation) & generation == "F1"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: gn-static-plot
#| eval: !expr gn_has_communities
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 14
gn_static_nodes <- tg |> activate(nodes) |> as_tibble()
gn_n_f1_highlighted <- sum(gn_static_nodes$is_f1 &
                              gn_static_nodes$community_gn_highlight != "other",
                            na.rm = TRUE)

# Palette keyed by the real cluster label text ggplot actually plots
# (community_label), built directly from tg's own data — not a
# re-keying of gn_community_colours (which is keyed by raw community
# ID), since that re-keying was fragile against community_label being
# a factor and produced an unreliable legend/colour match.
gn_label_colours <- gn_static_nodes |>
  distinct(community_gn_highlight, community_label) |>
  mutate(colour = gn_community_colours[as.character(community_gn_highlight)]) |>
  select(community_label, colour) |>
  tibble::deframe()

ggraph(tg, layout = "drl") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.05, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = community_label, size = community_gn_highlight != "other"),
                   alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_node_point(
    data = ~ dplyr::filter(.x, is_f1),
    shape = 21, colour = "black", fill = NA, stroke = 0.6, size = 3
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = gn_label_colours, name = "Cluster",
                       guide = guide_legend(ncol = 1)) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c("TRUE" = 1.6, "FALSE" = 0.6), guide = "none") +
  theme_graph() +
  theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 8)) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "Full citation graph, ", format(vcount(g), big.mark = ","), " nodes — ",
      gn_top_n, " largest Girvan-Newman clusters highlighted"
    ),
    subtitle = paste0(
      "(fragmentation-onset cut, round ", format(gn_earliest$round, big.mark = ","), "). ",
      "Black-ringed dots mark F1 papers (", gn_n_f1_highlighted, " within these clusters)."
    )
  )
```

Only the top `r gn_top_n` clusters are individually coloured; the
remaining `r format(gn_earliest$n_communities - gn_top_n, big.mark = ",")`
are grey. Beyond roughly `r gn_top_n` colours, a reader cannot reliably
distinguish them on the plot.


#### Internal structure of individual communities [TO BE COMPLETED]

The round-`r format(gn_earliest$round, big.mark = ",")` partition and the whole-graph dendrogram above both
describe the corpus at a single level: `r format(gn_earliest$n_communities, big.mark = ",")` communities, and one tree
covering the earliest few hundred splits across all of them together.
A separate question is whether any individual community has further
structure worth surfacing on its own, the same kind of check performed
earlier (see "Choosing a stopping point") for two clusters against
paper titles and annotation coding.

`gn_analysis/build_subcluster_trees.R` addresses this directly: seeded
from the real round-`r format(gn_earliest$round, big.mark = ",")` community membership (not a re-derived or
arbitrary starting point), it replays `removal_log.csv` separately for
each of the round's largest communities and records what happens to
each one afterward, run below using that same round so it can't drift
out of sync with the partition described above. An initial version
capped this replay at a fixed number of split events; that cap was
itself an arbitrary choice with no basis in the data, so the script
now replays each community to natural completion (full fragmentation
or the end of the log) by default.

```{r}
#| label: gn-subclusters-generate
#| eval: !expr gn_has_communities
#| results: hide
gn_subclusters_dir <- here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "subclusters")
gn_subcluster_summary_csv <- file.path(gn_subclusters_dir, "subcluster_summary.csv")

gn_subclusters_stale <- !file.exists(gn_subcluster_summary_csv) ||
  file.info(gn_subcluster_summary_csv)$mtime < file.info(gn_result_path)$mtime

if (gn_subclusters_stale) {
  dir.create(gn_subclusters_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  status <- system2(
    "Rscript",
    args = c(
      here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "build_subcluster_trees.R"),
      here("data", "citation_edgelist.csv"),
      here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "removal_log.csv"),
      gn_result_path,
      as.character(gn_earliest$round),
      gn_subclusters_dir,
      "3",                        # min_community_size, script's own default
      as.character(gn_top_n)      # max_trees — explicitly tied to gn_top_n
                                   # rather than relying on the script's
                                   # own default (12) to happen to match;
                                   # confirmed these had silently drifted
                                   # apart (gn_top_n = 20, script default
                                   # = 12) before this fix, so the prose's
                                   # "top gn_top_n communities" claim did
                                   # not match what was actually computed.
    )
  )
  if (status != 0) {
    warning("build_subcluster_trees.R exited with status ", status,
            "; subcluster figures may be missing or stale.")
  }
}
```

Doing so shows that, past each community's first split, every one of
the `r gn_top_n` largest communities collapses the same way the whole graph
does: a single dominant piece sheds one node at a time for hundreds of
further rounds, with no further balanced division anywhere in the
sequence. Plotted as a dendrogram, this produces the same long
single-branch shape for every community regardless of its size or its
first split, differing only in length, so the per-community dendrogram
plots turned out uninformative and are not included here (the script
still writes them; see `gn_analysis/results/subclusters/` if useful).

The one real signal in this data is the size of the two pieces at each
community's first split, plotted below. On this corpus, that pattern
is close to absolute, not just typical: every one of the `r gn_top_n`
largest communities sheds exactly one node at first split, with the
remaining piece staying fully intact. Any community whose two
pieces are closer in size is a candidate for the same kind of
title/annotation check performed earlier (see "Choosing a stopping
point"), and any community where the *smaller* piece is the one that
stays intact — rather than the one shed — runs against the pattern
seen in every other community here and in the previous version of this
corpus, and would be worth investigating further. Reading the specific
communities and split sizes that meet either description off the plot,
rather than naming them in prose here, keeps this section accurate
across re-runs against different partitions.

```{r}
#| label: gn-first-splits
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| eval: !expr file.exists(here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "subclusters", "subcluster_summary.csv"))
subcluster_summary <- read_csv(
  here("analysis", "gn_analysis", "results", "subclusters", "subcluster_summary.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

first_splits <- subcluster_summary |>
  filter(!is.na(first_split_sizes)) |>
  separate(first_split_sizes, into = c("piece_a", "piece_b"), sep = "/", convert = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    larger_piece  = pmax(piece_a, piece_b),
    smaller_piece = pmin(piece_a, piece_b)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(smaller_piece)) |>
  mutate(community_label = fct_reorder(paste("Community", community_id), smaller_piece))

first_splits_long <- first_splits |>
  select(community_label, larger_piece, smaller_piece) |>
  pivot_longer(c(larger_piece, smaller_piece), names_to = "piece", values_to = "size") |>
  mutate(piece = factor(piece, levels = c("larger_piece", "smaller_piece"),
                         labels = c("Larger piece", "Smaller piece")))

ggplot(first_splits_long, aes(x = size, y = community_label, fill = piece)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = size), position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3) +
  scale_x_log10(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Larger piece" = "#4C72B0", "Smaller piece" = "#DD8452")) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("First-split piece sizes, round ", format(gn_earliest$round, big.mark = ","),
                    "'s largest communities"),
    subtitle = "Sorted by size of the smaller piece; most balanced at top",
    x = "Nodes in each piece at first split (log scale)",
    y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**Not yet done.** Whichever community stands out above as the most
balanced split is the strongest remaining candidate for a
title/annotation check; whichever community shows the smaller-piece-
stays-intact anomaly is the strongest candidate for a different kind
of check. Neither has been carried out against this corpus's partition.

#### Cluster labeling

This section identifies each cluster's most-cited papers by
within-cluster citation degree, then has a language model write a
label and description from their titles, independent of the F1
annotation codebook. The pipeline takes a partition as input,
from any community-detection method at any cut, not just the
Girvan-Newman partition used above; it is documented here because this
is where a labeled partition currently exists to show. Comparison
against the codebook is `03_joined_descriptions.qmd`: a separate, later
step, so the two stay apart until then. Implemented as a standalone
pipeline in `cluster_labelling/` (same convention as `gn_analysis/`:
not part of this document's render chain).

For each cluster, the papers most cited by other members of that same
cluster are ranked and sampled, then labeled by an LLM: rationale, the
full step-by-step method, output format, and known limitations are all
in `cluster_labelling/README.md`, kept current there rather than
duplicated here.

**Results.**

```{r}
#| label: cluster-labels-table
#| echo: false
#| eval: !expr file.exists(here("analysis", "cluster_labelling", "results", "cluster_labels.csv"))
gn_cluster_labels_full <- read_csv(
  here("analysis", "cluster_labelling", "results", "cluster_labels.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# representatives.csv carries the within-cluster degree of each
# sampled paper, in rank order (see select_representatives.py) — reused
# here, not to show individual papers, but to derive, per cluster, the
# same hub-dominated classification select_representatives.py computes
# internally and only ever prints to console (never writes to a file):
# rank-1's within-cluster degree at least --hub-ratio-threshold (5.0,
# the script's own default) times rank-2's. cluster_size, also from
# this file, is the actual figure the labelling pipeline used, not a
# count recomputed independently here.
gn_reps_path <- here("analysis", "cluster_labelling", "results", "representatives.csv")
gn_cluster_shape <- if (file.exists(gn_reps_path)) {
  read_csv(gn_reps_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    group_by(community_id) |>
    summarise(
      cluster_size = first(cluster_size),
      shape = if (n() >= 2 && within_cluster_degree[2] > 0 &&
                  within_cluster_degree[1] / within_cluster_degree[2] >= 5.0) {
        "Hub-dominated"
      } else {
        "Distributed"
      },
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(community_id = as.character(community_id))
} else {
  tibble(community_id = character(), cluster_size = integer(), shape = character())
}

gn_cluster_labels_full |>
  mutate(community_id = as.character(community_id)) |>
  left_join(gn_cluster_shape, by = "community_id") |>
  arrange(desc(cluster_size)) |>
  transmute(
    `Cluster ID` = community_id,
    Size = cluster_size,
    Shape = coalesce(shape, "n/a"),
    Label = label,
    Description = description,
    `Secondary label` = coalesce(secondary_label, "")
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Every currently-labeled cluster, sorted largest first. Shape is
"Hub-dominated" where one paper's within-cluster citation degree is at
least 5 times the next-highest (`--hub-ratio-threshold`, per the
README), "Distributed" otherwise; "n/a" where `representatives.csv`
does not have this cluster's data. `unaccounted_titles`,
`groups_json`, and `titles_missing_from_groups`, internal verification
columns explained in the README, are omitted here; see the raw CSVs in
`cluster_labelling/results/` for those directly.
